title: Scientists Find New Giant Stick Insects Hiding in Plain Sight
summary:
Stick insects are masters of disguise. Their long, thin bodies look just like twigs. Now scientists in Australia have found that some of these insects fooled experts, too.

A research team from the University of Sydney took a fresh look at large Australian stick insects in a group called Anchiale. Scientists had thought this group in Australia contained just two species. The team found that there are actually five. They identified two new species and brought back a third species that had gone unrecognized for decades.

The insects live from northern New South Wales, along the coast of Queensland and into tropical northern Australia. People have reported more than 1,000 sightings of them on citizen science websites, and scientists have studied them for years. Still, the differences had been missed.

To sort them out, researchers used DNA tests, museum specimens, field surveys, sightings from the public and insects raised in captivity. One large stick insect that many people knew well turned out to have been misidentified for decades. It is now recognized as its own species, Anchiale robusta.

The team also described a new species, Anchiale mabiensis, from the endangered Mabi rainforest in Queensland. Its eggs have a special lid, something never recorded before in any stick insect or its closest relatives.

"Taxonomy is often a bit like detective work," said lead author Dr. Braxton Jones. Taxonomy is the science of naming and grouping living things.

The work could help farmers and foresters, too. One stick insect that sometimes strips leaves from trees turned out to be more than one species. The study was published in the journal Austral Entomology.
why_it_matters: Even well-studied insects can hide unknown species, so careful study helps scientists understand and protect nature and manage insects that affect farms and forests.

keywords.explanation: A species is a group of living things that are alike and can usually have young together.
Citizen science is when ordinary people help researchers by sharing observations, such as photos of animals.
Specimens are samples of plants or animals that are saved and studied, often in museums.
Misidentified means given the wrong name or mistaken for something else.
Endangered means at risk of disappearing forever.
Taxonomy is the science of naming and grouping living things.

background_read: Stick insects are plant-eating insects whose long, thin bodies help them hide by looking like twigs or branches.
Scientists group living things into species, which are kinds of organisms that share features and can usually breed with one another.
Because some species look almost the same, scientists compare DNA, museum specimens and details like eggs to tell them apart.
Australia has a huge variety of insects, and many have never been formally described by scientists.
